Pooled result

Estimate withdrawn. Two composites, not one estimand. Registered primaries read from ClinicalTrials.gov 2026-08-19. Fourier (NCT01764633, n=27,564) registers 'Time to Cardiovascular Death, Myocardial Infarction, Hospitalization for Unstable Angina, Stroke, or Coronary Revascularization'. Odyssey outcomes (NCT01663402, n=18,924) registers 'Time to First Occurrence of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Event (MACE)', defined in its own description as CHD death, non-fatal MI, fatal and non-fatal ischaemic stroke, or unstable angina requiring hospitalisation. They differ on three axes: fourier counts all cardiovascular death against odyssey's CHD death; Fourier counts all stroke against odyssey's ischaemic stroke; and fourier counts coronary revascularisation, which odyssey does not. Revascularisation is the highest-frequency component in this class of trial, so this is not a rounding difference in the event definition -- it changes what is being counted. P37: composite names are not definitions. Separately, the estimator was DerSimonian-Laird at k=2, and DL is refused below k=10 in this project because its tau-squared is badly biased with few studies. And the object already said so: it carried estimand_established=false and a poolable_reason stating the estimate had been recovered from the page rather than established. Authority: mecir Box 10.10.a C62 -- undertake or display a meta-analysis only if participants, interventions, comparisons and outcomes are judged sufficiently similar to ensure a clinically meaningful answer.

What this does not establish. Not that PCSK9 inhibition is ineffective -- both trials individually report reductions. Not that either trial is poor. Not that no poolable question exists here: a shared estimand may well be constructible from a component both trials report separately, and that is a build rather than a deletion. Only that this number, as pooled, does not estimate one quantity.

Does the answer depend on the pooling method?

With two or three studies the Cochrane Handbook (10.10.4.4–10.10.4.5) asks for a sensitivity analysis comparing interval methods rather than a choice between them. Both are given here; the published interval is the first row.

Table 7. Does the answer depend on the pooling method?
IntervalMethodSummary (95% CI)
as publishedDerSimonian-Laird inverse-variance on extracted effect estimates0.844 (0.7952 to 0.8959)
sensitivity (Handbook 10.10.4.5)REML with Hartung-Knapp, t on k-1 = 1 degree(s) of freedom (t = 12.7062)0.844 (0.5737 to 1.2418)

The published point is 0.8440 and the house-rule point is 0.8440. The number a reader remembers does not move; what differs is the precision claim. That is why nothing downstream catches this -- every memorable quantity survives.

A floor of 1 is applied to the variance-inflation factor so the adjustment can never narrow an interval below the unadjusted one. That guard is the recognised modification for exactly this instability, and its existence is evidence the small-k behaviour is a known problem with known handling rather than a novel judgement.

Limitations

What this review does not give a clinician: the number of events in each arm and any absolute effect or number needed to treat. A relative effect cannot be turned into the benefit or the risk facing one patient without them, so this review can support a judgement about what these trials found and not a judgement about what to do.1

Reporting guidelines

This review reports against PRISMA 2020. A screening record is held on this object and the flow it supports is shown in the Methods. The completed PRISMA checklist and FLOW diagram are not held here: the venue requires them deposited in an approved repository with a DOI cited in the Data Availability Statement, and minting that DOI is an author action rather than a build step.1
